title: Balak: a hired curse (Numbers 22:2–6)
hookLine: the king of Moab pays the prophet Balaam to curse Israel

lines: A PAID REVIEW, A FUNDED STUDY.
A FRIGHTENED KING, ACROSS THE HILL.
cards: A glowing review of a hotel, written by someone the hotel paid. A study about sugar, funded by a sugar company. Behind each one sits a plain question worth asking before believing anything: who's paying for this?
The Torah has a story built around that question. A new portion begins today, and for once the Israelites barely appear in it.
The whole story happens on the other side of the hill, where a frightened king is reaching for his wallet.

teach.b: Balak, son of Zippor, is king of Moab. He has seen what Israel did to the Amorites, and Moab is terrified.
In the text's vivid picture, paraphrased, this crowd will lick up everything around us the way an ox licks up the grass of the field. So Balak doesn't raise an army. He hires a curse.
He sends messengers to a seer named Balaam, son of Beor, who lives far off by the River: come and curse this people for me.

teach.h: HE WHOM THOU CURSEST IS CURSED.
teach.b: Then the flattery that sounds like a sales pitch, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "for I know that he whom thou blessest is blessed, and he whom thou cursest is cursed."
The elders set out with the fees for divination in their hands. Payment up front. Two surprises.
First, Balaam may not be only a character in a story.

Archaeologists at a site called Deir Alla, in Jordan, found an ancient plaster inscription that speaks of Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods. A seer by that name was remembered outside the Bible too.
Second, the rabbis read Balaam as someone whose gift was for sale.

In Pirkei Avot, they contrast the students of Abraham, who have a generous eye, a humble spirit and a modest appetite, with the students of Balaam, who have a grudging eye, a proud spirit and a greedy appetite.
And notice the portion's name, taken from its opening words. It isn't Balaam, after the prophet.

teach.h: NAMED FOR THE MAN WITH THE MONEY.
teach.b: It's Balak, the man with the money.

how: The portion of Balak is read in synagogue in the yearly cycle; its story is told almost entirely from outside the camp of Israel.

o: a Moabite word for a curse spoken for pay
the Moabite king who tried to hire a curse
the seer hired from far off by the River

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.

s: the portion is named after the prophet Balaam
it's named Balak, from its opening words: the king who paid.
an inscription outside the Bible mentions Balaam son of Beor
found at Deir Alla in Jordan, written on plaster.
Balak first gathered an army against Israel
he sent messengers to hire a curse instead.

games.q: you're a frightened king. a huge people is camped near your border. what's your plan?
o: pay a well-known seer to curse them.
games.why: Balak sends for Balaam with the fees for divination in hand: for I know that he whom thou blessest is blessed, and he whom thou cursest is cursed.

practice: Bring to mind one opinion you picked up recently, about a product, a person, the news, maybe even yourself, and trace it back to where it came from. Did someone gain by your believing it?
There's no need to be cynical, since many opinions are honest; just look for the hand on the wallet, if there is one, and then let the question go.

wordCard.voice: Balak. The king of Moab who tried to buy a curse, and the name of the portion that tells the story of the prophet he hired.

orig.note: Hebrew: Balak, son of Zippor, king of Moab, whose name the portion takes.

carryVoice: Your line: who's paying. It's worth asking before believing anything. That's day four hundred sixty-one.
